idiom_name: discriminated union + exhaustive switch with a never check (assertNever)
implementation_notes: TypeScript closes the set at the type level: a discriminated union of object literal types (type Shape = { kind: 'circle'; r: number } | ...) is the variant set, narrowing on the discriminant is checked by tsc, and exhaustiveness comes from assigning the residual value to never - or calling an assertNever(x: never): never helper - in the default arm, so a new union member turns that assignment into a compile error. That replaces the visitor structure: the members carry data only and each operation is one switch in the module that needs it. There is no runtime guarantee and no sealing beyond the type alias, so keep the classic OO form when the hierarchy is a published class API with methods; narrowing also needs strictNullChecks and literal discriminants.
pitfalls: assertNever is a compile-time trick with a runtime throw: a transpile-only pipeline (esbuild, ts-node, Babel) never runs the check, and without strictNullChecks narrowing is weaker, so the proof is only as strong as the type-check step in CI.
The discriminant must be a literal type present on every member; an optional, widened or inherited discriminant collapses narrowing and the never assignment stops failing when it should.
A default arm that returns a fallback instead of asserting re-opens the union silently, and a JSON cast bypasses the union entirely because the check is erased at run time.
